title: Healthy Versus Pathology Comparison
subtitle: Compare variation, dysfunction, injury and disorder without treating a scan as a diagnosis
altText: Accessible chalkboard-style comparison of two overlapping brain network maps: one shows variable healthy organisation and the other shows structural, functional, developmental, vascular and degenerative patterns, joined by a clinical-context bridge.
learningObjectives: Distinguish healthy variation, dysfunction, injury and disorder using clinical context rather than a binary normal-abnormal label.
Compare structural, functional, developmental, vascular and degenerative patterns without assuming that imaging establishes diagnosis.
Interpret symptoms through distributed networks, pathways, time course and reserve.
Identify limitations and uncertainty when relating a biological finding to a person's presentation.

sections.explainSimply: Healthy brains vary. A difference on a scan may be harmless, while important dysfunction may occur without a visible structural lesion. Pathology becomes clinically meaningful through pattern, time course, symptoms and context.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Variation describes differences within expected diversity; dysfunction is impaired operation; injury is damage caused by an event; disorder is a clinically defined syndrome involving distress, impairment or risk. These categories overlap but are not interchangeable, and none can be inferred from imaging alone.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Comparison requires converging evidence from history, examination, cognitive or psychological assessment, laboratory data, structural and functional imaging, longitudinal change and differential diagnosis. Structural abnormalities may be incidental; functional changes may be state-dependent or nonspecific; developmental organisation may differ without representing acquired damage; vascular lesions follow time and territory; degenerative disease is supported by progressive clinical and biomarker patterns. Network disconnection, diaschisis, compensation, reserve and comorbidity shape phenotype.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A city map and a traffic report: street layout, current flow, construction damage and long-term decline describe different things, and none alone tells you how one resident is functioning.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Careful framing prevents biological essentialism, false reassurance from an unremarkable scan, and overdiagnosis from incidental findings. It supports formulation that integrates cognition, emotion, behaviour, daily function, development and medical context.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Acute infarction can disrupt a vascularly organised network; traumatic axonal injury can disconnect systems beyond a focal lesion; epilepsy, migraine or metabolic disturbance can alter function transiently; developmental differences shape network organisation; degeneration evolves across connected systems. Similar symptoms can arise through different mechanisms, and similar findings can have different consequences.
sections.clinicalPearl: Treat imaging as one source of evidence: ask whether the finding, time course, network and examination converge before attributing a symptom or diagnosis.
sections.practicalExample: Compare an incidental small arachnoid cyst in a well person, transient network dysfunction during migraine aura, focal tissue injury after an MCA infarct, a developmental language disorder and progressive medial temporal-network degeneration. The clinically useful distinction comes from convergence, not appearance alone.
sections.limitationsCautions: Normal ranges depend on age, development, acquisition method and reference population. Group-level biomarkers often overlap across individuals and diagnoses. Absence of a visible lesion does not exclude dysfunction, while an abnormal-looking finding may be incidental. Avoid value-laden language and deterministic normal-versus-abnormal conclusions.

anatomy.position: Whole-brain comparison across cortex, subcortex, white matter, vascular territories and large-scale functional networks.
anatomy.spatialRelationships: Local tissue findings sit within connected systems; remote effects may occur through white-matter disconnection, diaschisis, altered excitation-inhibition balance and compensatory recruitment.
outputs: need for monitoring or urgent action
anatomy.bloodSupply: Vascular change is interpreted by onset, arterial territory, collateral supply and tissue evolution. Chronic small-vessel disease and incidental vascular variants require clinical correlation.
anatomy.lesionEffects: Effects depend on lesion mechanism, location, volume, laterality, white-matter involvement, distributed network disruption, premorbid reserve and recovery; a lesion does not map one-to-one onto a symptom.
psychologicalPresentations: distress shaped by interpretation and context
no impairment despite an incidental finding
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: A healthy-pathology comparison can organise hypotheses and urgency, but diagnosis requires concordance among clinical phenotype, course, examination and appropriately interpreted tests.

explorerParts.label: Healthy variation & reserve
explorerParts.detail: Brain morphology, lateralisation, connectivity and performance vary with age, development, experience and measurement conditions.
explorerParts.clinical: Use appropriate norms and functional evidence before labelling a variant pathological.

explorerParts.label: Structural change
explorerParts.detail: Atrophy, mass effect, altered signal, malformation or white-matter change describes structure, not by itself cause, severity or diagnosis.
explorerParts.clinical: Correlate location and chronicity with symptoms; consider incidental findings, artefact and alternative causes.

explorerParts.label: Functional dysfunction
explorerParts.short: Operation can change without a fixed lesion
explorerParts.detail: Network physiology can vary with seizure activity, migraine, medication, sleep, pain, metabolic state and psychiatric state.
explorerParts.clinical: Functional measures are often state-dependent and group-derived; they should support rather than replace clinical assessment.

explorerParts.label: Developmental difference
explorerParts.detail: Developmental timing, plasticity and experience shape network organisation and skill acquisition across childhood and adulthood.
explorerParts.clinical: Establish developmental history and adaptive impact; avoid describing all atypical organisation as damage.

explorerParts.label: Vascular injury
explorerParts.detail: Ischaemia and haemorrhage disrupt tissue according to vessel anatomy, collateral flow, lesion evolution and connected pathways.
explorerParts.clinical: Sudden focal deficits require urgent stroke assessment; imaging pattern assists but does not replace bedside evaluation.

explorerParts.label: Degenerative network change
explorerParts.detail: Neurodegenerative processes often spread through vulnerable cell populations and connected networks rather than respecting one isolated region.
explorerParts.clinical: Diagnosis depends on progressive phenotype, exclusion of mimics and, when appropriate, validated biomarkers.

quiz.question: Which statement best distinguishes an imaging finding from a diagnosis?
options: A finding becomes diagnostic only when appropriately combined with clinical and other evidence
Functional imaging independently establishes psychiatric diagnosis
quiz.rationale: Imaging is one evidence source; diagnosis depends on validated criteria and convergence with phenotype, course and examination.

quiz.question: Which description of dysfunction is most accurate?
options: Impaired operation may occur with or without a visible structural lesion
It always means irreversible tissue destruction
It is identical to a disorder
It can be inferred from one group-average biomarker
quiz.rationale: Physiological dysfunction may be transient, state-dependent or structurally occult and is not synonymous with injury or disorder.

quiz.question: Why can similar lesions produce different outcomes?
options: Network extent, laterality, reserve, development, comorbidity and recovery differ
Every symptom belongs to one brain region
quiz.rationale: Clinical effects emerge from distributed systems and individual context, not lesion location alone.

quiz.question: What most strongly supports a degenerative interpretation?
options: A progressive clinical phenotype with a concordant longitudinal pattern and appropriate exclusion of mimics
quiz.rationale: Degenerative diagnosis rests on progression and converging clinical evidence, sometimes supported by validated biomarkers.
